Except regarding forbidden fats and illicit relations where he derived physical pleasure, and in human bodily pleasure it is impossible that there was not some minute hidden intent at least, for by nature a person senses his pleasure even if he is unaware of it in his conscious memory.

So here: the generation of the Dispersion was budding, desiring the settlement of the world, wherefore Noah sought to banish anger to stabilize society — the reverse of the Flood generation who cared nothing for civilization, content with fleeting pleasure.

column9: Sotah 21a: ‘The Gemara asks: Does the merit of a mitzva protect one so much as to delay her punishment? column13: This is why these conquering nations are mentioned in the verse: “The Caphtorim who came out of Caphtor destroyed them, etc.” For although the Caphtorim possessed less raw physical power, because they had greater free will to govern their bodies, they conquered the earlier inhabitants; since one endowed with moral choice can overcome one who lacks choice; culminating in Israel, the masters of conscious free will, who possess the spiritual capacity to elevate and conquer the entire world.

column9: Eikhah Rabbah 4:25: “The Midrash relates concerning the custom of kindling lights: when a child was born they lit lamps in celebration, and when a child passed away or fell silent on Chanukah they kindled lamps to signify that the light of the soul and the light of the mitzvah endure beyond physical darkness.” Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 24 — Menasseh and Ephraim: The Eight Lights and Thanksgiving, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Eikhah Rabbah 4:25) to illuminate his statement here (“and so we find in Midrash Rabbah (Eichah 4:100): "The child fell silent on Chanukah, etc., and when a child died they lit lamps, etc."; and therefore here too, when they saw the miracle they kindled lamps, and this...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.

column11: And Rashi explained [s.v. Minhag], and this is his wording: "And the practical difference is that it does not require a blessing, for one cannot say 'and commanded us,' since it is not even included within 'You shall not deviate'"; thus far his words. And so is explicit in the Gemara there: A certain man brought a willow before Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Tzadok; he beat it and did not recite a blessing, holding that it is a custom of the prophets.

column13: And behold, the power of reproduction generated in the human form, and especially in the birth of a male child, is channeled from the influx of the Name Havayah; and from this is born a creature capable of expanding and generating further on its own; and therefore, since procreation issuing from the male force derives from the essential light of Hashem, it is impossible for birth to occur except through forgetfulness and concealment, entirely beyond human conscious intellect, purely from the essential light and power of Hashem.
